title: Episode 316: Elizabeth I (Part 2): Mary Queen of Scots, the Earl of Essex, and the Shakespearean Sunset
description:
The dramatic second half of Queen Elizabeth I's legendary reign. For nineteen years, Elizabeth held her charismatic, Catholic cousin Mary, Queen of Scots, in honorable English captivity. When Sir Francis Walsingham's web of codebreakers trapped Mary in the Babington assassination plot, Elizabeth wrestled with the terrifying precedent of executing an anointed queen. Surrounding herself with artistic luminaries during the flowering of Shakespeare and Marlowe, Elizabeth's final years were tormented by the treasonous rebellion of her youthful favorite, the Earl of Essex. Standing before Parliament to deliver her transcendent 'Golden Speech', discover the poignant twilight of Gloriana.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series concludes our two-part saga of Queen Elizabeth I: exploring the tragic rivalry with Mary Queen of Scots, the treason of her beloved Essex, and the glorious cultural sunset of the Tudor dynasty. Here is George with part two of the Virgin Queen.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE RIVAL QUEEN: MARY STUART'S FLIGHT TO ENGLAND: 1568
For nineteen years, Elizabeth's greatest domestic and international danger was embodied in her glamorous, Catholic cousin, Mary Queen of Scots. Granddaughter of Henry VIII's sister Margaret Tudor, Mary had been Queen of France and Queen of Scotland, claiming the English throne as legitimate heir. In 1567, Mary's scandalous Scottish reign collapsed following the mysterious gunpowder murder of her husband, Lord Darnley, and her subsequent marriage to his suspected assassin, the Earl of Bothwell. Deposed by Scottish Protestant lords, Mary made a desperate, fateful escape across the Solway Firth in a fishing boat in May 1568, landing in northern England to seek Elizabeth's protection. For Elizabeth, Mary's arrival was an insoluble political dilemma: to restore Mary to Scotland by force was dangerous; to allow her to go to Catholic France was suicidal; and to keep her in England made Mary an irresistible magnet for Catholic conspiracies to assassinate Elizabeth and seize the crown. Elizabeth placed Mary in comfortable, closely guarded captivity in northern castles like Tutbury and Sheffield, where Mary spent two decades embroidering tapestries and plotting her liberation. Mary Queen of Scots' nineteen years of captivity in England were a prolonged exercise in royal claustrophobia: moved between cold, damp midland castles under the strict custody of the Earl of Shrewsbury, Mary watched her radiant youth wither away in chronic rheumatism and despair. Yet she maintained a royal court in miniature, employing French secretaries, embroiderers, and physicians, using secret ciphers concealed in shoe heels and beer casks to correspond with the Duke of Guise, King Philip II, and Catholic agents in Rome, forever convinced that God would deliver her from her heretic cousin's clutches.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: WALSINGHAM'S WEB OF SPIES: THE BABINGTON PLOT: 1586
Elizabeth's survival against relentless Catholic assassination plots was orchestrated by Sir Francis Walsingham, England's brilliant, puritanical Spymaster General. Operating a sophisticated network of fifty secret agents, double-crossers, and cryptographers across Europe, Walsingham uncovered conspiracy after conspiracy: the Northern Rebellion of 1569, the Ridolfi Plot of 1571, and the Throckmorton Plot of 1583. But Walsingham needed indisputable, smoking-gun evidence directly implicating Mary Stuart. In 1586, he orchestrated an elaborate trap: Anthony Babington, a wealthy young Catholic gentleman, devised a conspiracy to assassinate Elizabeth and rescue Mary with foreign troops. Walsingham allowed Babington's secret letters to be smuggled into Mary's residence at Chartley inside waterproof beer barrels. Walsingham's master cryptanalyst, Thomas Phelippes, intercepted, decoded, and copied every letter before sending them on. In July 1586, Mary made her fatal error: replying in cipher to Babington, she explicitly endorsed the assassination of Elizabeth. Walsingham had his trap; Babington and his conspirators were arrested, hanged, and quartered, and Mary was put on trial. Sir Francis Walsingham's counter-intelligence operation was the forerunner of the modern Secret Intelligence Service. Walsingham understood that Anthony Babington was a vain, gullible fanatic; he deliberately recruited the beer brewer of Burton-on-Trent to serve as a double agent, carrying waterproof leather pouches of letters inside the bungs of ale casks delivered to Mary's cellar. Walsingham's codebreaker Thomas Phelippes not only deciphered Mary's fatal letter approving Elizabeth's assassination, but forged a brilliant postscript in Mary's own cipher asking Babington to supply the names of the six gentlemen sworn to kill Elizabeth, enabling the Crown to arrest the entire conspiracy in a single nocturnal sweep.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: FOTHERINGHAY CASTLE: THE EXECUTION OF MARY STUART: FEBRUARY 8, 1587
In October 1586, Mary was tried for high treason at Fotheringhay Castle in Northamptonshire before thirty-six English peers. Denied legal counsel or access to her papers, Mary defended herself with magnificent royal eloquence, denying the jurisdiction of an English court over an anointed sovereign. She was found guilty. For four agonizing months, Elizabeth hesitated to sign the death warrant, terrified of establishing the precedent of regicide and dreading the divine wrath of kings. When she finally signed the warrant in February 1587, she instructed her secretary William Davison not to dispatch it, hoping Mary would die quietly of illness. But her council dispatched the warrant secretly. On February 8, 1587, Mary walked into the Great Hall of Fotheringhay. Shedding her outer black gown, she stood revealed in petticoats of brilliant crimson—the liturgical color of Catholic martyrdom. Blindfolded with a gold-embroidered handkerchief, Mary laid her head on the block. It took three clumsy blows of the ax to sever her head; when the executioner lifted it shouting 'God save the Queen!', her auburn wig came off in his hand, revealing cropped gray hair, while her loyal little pet lapdog emerged trembling from beneath her voluminous skirts. Mary Stuart's execution at Fotheringhay Castle was an extraordinary act of liturgical theater: by shedding her black gown to reveal scarlet undergarments, she proclaimed to European Christendom that she was dying as a Catholic martyr for the Holy Faith, not as a convicted traitor. When Elizabeth learned that her council had dispatched the warrant without her final authorization, the queen erupted in hysterical fury, banishing William Cecil from court for four months and throwing her unfortunate secretary William Davison into the Tower of London, maintaining to foreign ambassadors the diplomatic fiction that she was entirely innocent of her royal cousin's blood.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE FLOWERING OF THE ENGLISH RENAISSANCE: SHAKESPEARE AND MARLOWE
Following the defeat of the Spanish Armada, England entered a cultural renaissance of astonishing brilliance, centered on the energetic, expanding metropolis of London. The theater became the vibrant democratic heart of the realm: on the Southbank of the Thames, open-air playhouses like the Globe, the Rose, and the Curtain drew thousands of spectators daily, from apprentice boys standing in the pit to noble courtiers. Christopher Marlowe revolutionized English dramatic verse with his mighty line in Tamburlaine and Doctor Faustus. William Shakespeare arrived from Stratford-upon-Avon, crafting his immortal comedies, histories, and tragedies. Elizabeth was an ardent patron of the stage, maintaining her own royal acting troupe, the Queen's Men, and summoning Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men, to perform plays like A Midsummer Night's Dream and The Merry Wives of Windsor at court during Christmas revels. Concurrently, English music reached its golden peak under William Byrd and Thomas Morley, while Edmund Spenser published his epic Arthurian allegory, The Faerie Queene, celebrating Elizabeth as the divine goddess Gloriana. The London theater of the 1590s was an unprecedented melting pot of English language and society: in playhouses like the Globe, seating up to three thousand people, citizens ate apples and cracked hazelnuts in the yard while listening to the sublime poetry of Hamlet, Henry V, and Romeo and Juliet. Shakespeare was intimately attuned to the queen's courtly politics: his depiction of the aging, deposed Richard II reflected contemporary anxieties about the succession, while his Merry Wives of Windsor was allegedly written at Elizabeth's personal royal command, wanting to see the fat knight Sir John Falstaff in love.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TRAGIC FAVORITE: ROBERT DEVEREUX, EARL OF ESSEX: 1599
In the twilight of her life, with her oldest advisors William Cecil and Leicester dead, the aging queen sought emotional vitality in the company of Robert Devereux, second Earl of Essex, Leicester's charismatic, hot-headed stepson. Thirty-three years her junior, Essex was handsome, reckless, and hungry for military glory. But Essex mistook the queen's indulgent affection for weakness. In 1598, during a heated Privy Council debate over Ireland, when Elizabeth mocked his recommendation, Essex turned his back on the queen in insolent contempt. Elizabeth struck him across the ear, shouting: 'Go and be hanged!' Essex instinctively reached for the hilt of his sword, shouting that he would not have taken such an insult from Henry VIII himself. Though reconciled, the rift was fatal. In 1599, Essex was given command of England's largest army to suppress Hugh O'Neill's rebellion in Ireland. Instead of fighting, Essex knighted dozens of his friends, concluded an unauthorized truce with O'Neill, and deserted his post, galloping to London and bursting mud-spattered into Elizabeth's private bedchamber before she was wigged or gowned, seeing the sixty-six-year-old queen in her bare vulnerability. Essex's disastrous campaign in Ireland during the Nine Years' War was a masterclass in military incompetence: provided with sixteen thousand veteran foot soldiers and thirteen hundred horsemen—the largest army England had fielded in the sixteenth century—Essex marched aimlessly across the bogs of Munster, losing three-quarters of his men to dysentery and desertion without fighting a single pitched battle. When he met the rebel leader Hugh O'Neill at a ford on the River Lagan, Essex negotiated a humiliating private truce in mid-stream, abandoning royal policy before deserting his post and galloping to London to force his way into the queen's bedchamber.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE ESSEX REBELLION AND THE SCAFFOLD ON TOWER GREEN: FEBRUARY 1601
Placed under house arrest and stripped of his lucrative royal monopoly on sweet wines, Essex's pride turned to desperate madness. Surrounding himself with disaffected young aristocrats and puritan soldiers at Essex House on the Strand, Essex plotted an armed coup to storm Whitehall, depose Elizabeth's ministers, and dictate the succession. On February 7, 1601, Essex's supporters paid the Lord Chamberlain's Men forty shillings to perform Shakespeare's Richard II at the Globe Theater, hoping the staged deposition of an English monarch would incite the populace. The next morning, Essex rode into the City of London with two hundred armed followers, shouting: 'For the Queen! A plot is laid for my life!' But Londoners shut their doors and ignored him; the herald proclaimed him a traitor, and royal troops surrounded Essex House with artillery. Essex surrendered, was tried for high treason in Westminster Hall, and condemned to death. On February 25, 1601, the thirty-four-year-old Earl was privately beheaded on Tower Green. Elizabeth sat in her private apartments, plucking melancholy tunes upon her virginal as the execution ax fell, her heart broken by the betrayal of her last favorite. Essex's trial in Westminster Hall was a bitter clash of former friends: Sir Francis Bacon, whose legal career Essex had generously funded with gifts of land, served as the Crown's prosecutor, coldly dissecting Essex's treason and comparing him to the Duke of Guise. On the scaffold on Tower Green, Essex was dressed in black velvet and satin, delivering a penitent confession before laying his head upon the block. It took three strokes of the ax to sever his neck. Elizabeth never recovered from the tragedy; she kept Essex's ring in a velvet-lined casket, withdrawing into prolonged bouts of silent weeping in her private apartments.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GOLDEN SPEECH AND THE PASSING OF GLORIANA: 1603
In November 1601, facing parliamentary discontent over royal economic monopolies, sixty-eight-year-old Elizabeth summoned the House of Commons to Whitehall to deliver her final, transcendent masterpiece of statecraft: the 'Golden Speech'. With poetic majesty, the queen told her kneeling MPs: 'Though God hath raised me high, yet this I count the glory of my crown, that I have reigned with your loves... I do not so much rejoice that God hath made me to be a queen, as to be a queen over so thankful a people.' In early 1603, grief at the death of her lifelong friend, the Countess of Nottingham, plunged the queen into profound melancholy. Refusing to eat or take to her bed, fearing she would never rise, Elizabeth stood propped on cushions for four consecutive days and nights at Richmond Palace, staring at the floor in silent meditation. Finally carried to her bed, she gestured with her hands when asked about the succession, confirming King James VI of Scotland as her rightful heir. On March 24, 1603, at three in the morning, seventy-year-old Queen Elizabeth I died peacefully in her sleep. The Tudor dynasty was ended; England and Scotland were united under a single crown, and the Elizabethan Golden Age passed into legend. In her final days at Richmond Palace, Elizabeth's refusal to lie down was born of a fierce warrior pride: she knew that once a monarch lay in bed, the court would abandon her to pay court to the rising Scottish heir. For four days, the seventy-year-old queen stood upright upon the carpets, propped by cushions, her eyes fixed upon the floor in profound contemplation. When her lifelong coronation ring had to be filed from her swollen finger, court observers wept, realizing that the sacred marriage between Elizabeth and the realm of England had finally reached its end. Her death closed the grandest epoch in English history, leaving a legacy of national independence, naval mastery, and sublime literature that would echo through the centuries.
